newsitem.title: USA: US OPTIONS FOCUS/STOCKS COULD RECOVER NEXT WEEK.
newsitem.headline: US OPTIONS FOCUS/STOCKS COULD RECOVER NEXT WEEK.

text.p: If history is any guide, U.S. stocks could recover next week, when August stock index and equity options expire.
Options traders noted Friday as the stock market dropped sharply that more often than not, stocks move higher during expiration weeks.
"Today is going to be a lead in to next week, but next week's going to be up," said one S&P 500 futures options trader said. "Every expiration the market seems to rally."
But by about 1230 CDT/1730 GMT, a rally looked difficult as September S&P 500 futures were down 20.25 points at 936.
The cash S&P 500 .SPX lost 19.31 to 931.88 and the bellwether Dow Jones Industrial Average .DJI was down 155 points at 8,033.
September S&P 500 futures were off their 926.75 session low, the SPX was off its 925.74 intraday low and the Dow was above its 7,976 session low.

Gregory Nie, a technical analyst at EVEREN Securities in Chicago, said the market's technical indicators were not in that bad shape going into Friday's rout, which was helped along by a steep drop in bond prices.
"It looks like this can be a temporary episode," he said, adding that Monday's action will clarify the picture.
He explained if there is follow-through selling Monday, it could turn momentum indicators bearish and suggest a change in the longer-term pattern.

Sellers have not been able to establish momentum to the downside when the market has experienced a sharp one-day decline but if they are able to do so this time, "that's a change you better pay attention to," Nie said.

The sell-off in stocks helped push volatilities in major U.S. stock index options higher, led by the Chicago Board Options Exchange's volatility index .VIX, which was up 4.8 points, or 23 percent, at 25.72.
One trader in OEX options said most of the action there was investors buying puts and selling calls on the way down.
"There seems to be a lot of one-way trading," he said. "It seems fairly liquid for the way it's been lately. There hasn't been much trouble getting things done."
The S&P 500 futures-options trader said the activity was orderly with no signs of a panic developing.
"This is a very uniform breakdown," he said.
He added that a couple firms were selling puts early on as the market declined but that as the session wore on there did not appear to be a large bias one way or the other.
Jerry Hegarty, an options analyst at Thomson Financial Services, said index put buying continued heavy, which was a good contrarian sign for a rebound next week.
But on chances of a recovery, he said: "We haven't even let the down move play out yet.
"It's just too early to start talking about when can it rally without knowing the extent of the decline," he said.
((Gregory Crawford, 312 408 8750))
